Participants provided informed consent, and the study was approved by the institutional review board of Reichman University (formerly the Interdisciplinary Center Herzliya).

Several months before the lab session, participants had completed a battery of surveys for course credit, including a trait-resilience questionnaire still in development (see the supplemental material).

In the lab, participants completed two 3-min trials in which they generated words of at least three letters from a 5 × 5 letter matrix, with bonus points for longer words; Trial 2 used a different matrix.

After Trial 2, participants completed a nine-item measure of overall need satisfaction (Deci & Ryan, 2000), along with measures of intrinsic motivation (McAuley et al., 1989) and vitality (Ryan & Frederick, 1997), and were then debriefed about the study's purpose and the false physiological feedback.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: This study was not preregistered. However, it tests the central hypotheses of the first author's thesis proposal, which was approved before data collection began. The analyses reported here are a reanalysis of the thesis data: the thesis analyzed change scores as a function of need condition and compared high-and low-resilience groups. We chose the baseline-adjusted ANCOVA as the primary analysis, since it is the recommended and more powerful approach for randomized pretest-posttest designs (van Breukelen, 2006; Vickers & Altman, 2001) and report the change-score and repeated-measures results as sensitivity analyses. A priori G*Power calculations for the originally planned mixed design (Cohen's f = .25, α = .05, power = .80, correlation between repeated measures = .50) indicated a minimum sample size of 120 for the between-subjects effect, the larger of the design's estimates. Consequently, 121 participants were included, all retained, and there were no interim analyses or stopping rules. Because the resilience scale is still in development and has not been validated, the resilience analyses are reported as exploratory in the supplement. Sensitivity benchmarks appear in the supplement.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/qwen3.5:4b' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Self-determination theory proposes that environments supporting the basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness foster autonomous motivation, engagement, wellbeing, and effective functioning.
Yet experimental evidence that a need-supportive context affects subsequent performance remains limited.
In a randomized experiment, undergraduates (N = 121) completed two trials of a timed word-generation task used as a behavioral performance indicator.
Between trials, an experimenter delivered a scripted, multicomponent manipulation intended to support or thwart these needs, or a neutral control interaction, followed by a stress induction.
In an analysis of covariance with HC3 standard errors, condition predicted Trial 2 performance after adjustment for Trial 1.
Participants in the need-supportive condition outperformed those in the neutral control, whereas the thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise.
These findings provide experimental evidence that a brief need-supportive context can carry over to subsequent performance under stress.
A Brief Need-Supportive Manipulation and Subsequent Task Performance: A Randomized Experiment Can social circumstances shape how well people perform?
Self-determination theory (SDT) proposes that social environments shape people's motivation and functioning (Deci & Ryan, 2000).
text.formatted: Self-determination theory (SDT) proposes that social environments shape people's motivation and functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Deci & Ryan, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Within SDT, three basic psychological needs are identified as fundamental: autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
Autonomy refers to volition and self-endorsement, competence to feeling effective and capable of mastery, and relatedness to feeling significant and connected.

Environments that support the satisfaction of these needs are expected to promote autonomous motivation, engagement, persistence, well-being, and effective functioning, while need thwarting, leading to need frustration, is associated with disengagement and ill-being (Vansteenkiste et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Environments that support the satisfaction of these needs are expected to promote autonomous motivation, engagement, persistence, well-being, and effective functioning, while need thwarting, leading to need frustration, is associated with disengagement and ill-being <ref type="bibr">(Vansteenkiste et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Need support and active need thwarting should not be treated as opposite ends of a single continuum.
An absence of need support should be distinguished from active need thwarting, such as pressure or rejection.
Likewise, need satisfaction and need frustration are empirically distinguishable experiences (Chen et al., 2015; Vansteenkiste et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Likewise, need satisfaction and need frustration are empirically distinguishable experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Chen et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vansteenkiste et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A large meta-analysis linked interpersonal need support with more favorable motivation and well-being and with small-to-moderate positive associations with performance (Slemp et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A large meta-analysis linked interpersonal need support with more favorable motivation and well-being and with small-to-moderate positive associations with performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Slemp et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, much of the evidence relating need support to performance remains correlational.

The closest experimental evidence comes from studies using timed word-generation tasks on two trials. Sheldon and Filak (2008) presented participants with instructions varying in taskrelated autonomy, competence, and relatedness and compared task performance.
text.formatted: The closest experimental evidence comes from studies using timed word-generation tasks on two trials. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Sheldon and Filak (2008)</ref> presented participants with instructions varying in taskrelated autonomy, competence, and relatedness and compared task performance.

text.text: Their performance models adjusted for initial task performance, but the experimental need-varying scripts began before that initial trial, meaning it was not a pre-manipulation baseline. Szulawski et al. (2021) manipulated bundled need support or frustration together with reward.
text.formatted: Their performance models adjusted for initial task performance, but the experimental need-varying scripts began before that initial trial, meaning it was not a pre-manipulation baseline. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Szulawski et al. (2021)</ref> manipulated bundled need support or frustration together with reward.

text.text: Their manipulations preceded both task trials, performance was summed across trials, and the design included no neutral condition.
Findings were mixed.

Sheldon and Filak found an effect of relatedness support in their factorial analysis, although neither relatedness condition differed significantly from neutral, whereas Szulawski et al. reported higher summed performance under bundled support than frustration.
However, neither study combined a pre-manipulation performance baseline with separate comparisons of need-supportive and need-thwarting interpersonal conditions against a neutral condition.

It therefore remains unclear whether needsupportive or need-thwarting interactions affect subsequent performance relative to a neutral interaction after accounting for baseline performance (i.e., performance measured before manipulation exposure).

The present study addressed this question by having participants complete an initial performance trial before exposure to a need-supportive, neutral-control, or need-thwarting interpersonal condition.
Participants then underwent a stress induction, followed by a second trial.
This allowed post-manipulation performance to be evaluated while accounting for premanipulation performance, and the stress manipulation further challenges the effect of the interpersonal context.

We predicted that participants in the need-supportive condition would show higher baseline-adjusted performance than those in the neutral-control condition (H1), whereas participants in the need-thwarting condition would show lower baseline-adjusted performance than those in the neutral-control condition (H2).
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
The sample consisted of 121 psychology undergraduates who participated to fulfill a research-participation requirement.
Because the task is language based, participants were required to have Hebrew as their first language and no diagnosed dyslexia or learning disability.
Most were first-year students (95.9%); 77.7% were female, and age ranged from 19 to 29 years (M = 22.98, SD = 1.66).
For random assignment, Qualtrics displayed the three condition labels in randomized order before each session, and the experimenter implemented the first-listed condition.
This resulted in 42 participants allocated to the need-supportive condition, 41 to the neutral control, and 38 to the need-thwarting condition.
The lead researcher and three trained research assistants used standardized scripts, and each administered all three conditions.
Experimenters were aware of condition assignment, but Trial 1 was completed before any condition-specific content was delivered.
Participants provided informed consent, and the study was approved by the institutional review board of Reichman University (formerly the Interdisciplinary Center Herzliya).
Figure 1 outlines the procedure (see supplementary for full detail and scripts).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> outlines the procedure (see supplementary for full detail and scripts).

text.text: Following the studies reviewed above, performance was indexed with a timed Hebrew word-generation task based on Boggle.

Several months before the lab session, participants had completed a battery of surveys for course credit, including a trait-resilience questionnaire still in development (see the supplemental material).

In the lab, participants completed two 3-min trials in which they generated words of at least three letters from a 5 × 5 letter matrix, with bonus points for longer words; Trial 2 used a different matrix.
Responses were scored according to the task rules (see the supplemental material).
The task score was the primary outcome, or dependent variable.

After Trial 1, the experimenter delivered the assigned interpersonal need-manipulation (adapted from Sheldon & Filak, 2008, through the Hebrew version of Kanat-Maymon et al., 2015, which we further adapted for this study).
text.formatted: After Trial 1, the experimenter delivered the assigned interpersonal need-manipulation (adapted from <ref type="bibr">Sheldon & Filak, 2008, through</ref> the Hebrew version of Kanat-Maymon et al., 2015, which we further adapted for this study).

text.text: In brief, need-supportive participants received favorable comparative feedback, chose which task to perform next from two sealed envelopes (both contained the same word-generation task), were addressed as unique individuals whose experiences mattered, and heard, "I'm sure you'll do very well."

Need-thwarting participants received unfavorable and belittling false feedback, saw the choice withdrawn, were told that their individual experience was unimportant, and heard, "You might get lucky this time" (i.e., might do better by chance).
Neutral-control participants received a new answer sheet and a brief reminder of the task rules, without comparative feedback, choice, personalization, or an expectancy statement.
The manipulation thus deliberately combined autonomy-, competence-, and relatedness-relevant features.
All participants then received the same stress induction before Trial 2: the experimenter attached skin conductance sensors to two of their fingertips and feigned alarm at the supposed reading.
No physiological data were recorded.
After supposedly contemplating how to proceed, the experimenter then asked participants to complete Trial 2 for the time being.
Trial 2 was identical to Trial 1 except for the new letter matrix.

After Trial 2, participants completed a nine-item measure of overall need satisfaction (Deci & Ryan, 2000), along with measures of intrinsic motivation (McAuley et al., 1989) and vitality (Ryan & Frederick, 1997), and were then debriefed about the study's purpose and the false physiological feedback.
text.formatted: After Trial 2, participants completed a nine-item measure of overall need satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Deci & Ryan, 2000)</ref>, along with measures of intrinsic motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(McAuley et al., 1989)</ref> and vitality <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ryan & Frederick, 1997)</ref>, and were then debriefed about the study's purpose and the false physiological feedback.

text.text: The analysis predicted Trial 2 performance from Trial 1 performance and randomized need condition, with neutral control as the reference and HC3 heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors.
The omnibus condition test was followed by supportive-versus-neutral and thwarting-versus-neutral contrasts.
Holm correction covered these two focal contrasts and a third contrast comparing the supportive condition with the average of the other conditions.
Contrast weights and their rationale appear in the supplement.
All tests were two-sided.
Unstandardized adjusted differences, 95% confidence intervals, and outcome-standardized contrasts are reported.
Covariate, scoring, bootstrap, influence, change-score, repeated-measures, and exploratory resilience analyses are reported in the supplement.
Analyses were performed in R (4.4.2; R Core Team, 2024).
This study was not preregistered.
However, it tests the central hypotheses of the first author's thesis proposal, which was approved before data collection began.
The analyses reported here are a reanalysis of the thesis data: the thesis analyzed change scores as a function of need condition and compared high-and low-resilience groups.

We chose the baseline-adjusted ANCOVA as the primary analysis, since it is the recommended and more powerful approach for randomized pretest-posttest designs (van Breukelen, 2006; Vickers & Altman, 2001) and report the change-score and repeated-measures results as sensitivity analyses.

text.text: A priori G*Power calculations for the originally planned mixed design (Cohen's f = .25, α = .05, power = .80, correlation between repeated measures = .50) indicated a minimum sample size of 120 for the between-subjects effect, the larger of the design's estimates.
Consequently, 121 participants were included, all retained, and there were no interim analyses or stopping rules.
Because the resilience scale is still in development and has not been validated, the resilience analyses are reported as exploratory in the supplement.
Sensitivity benchmarks appear in the supplement.

text.text: Trial 1 strongly predicted Trial 2 performance (β = .62, 95% CI [.47, .77], p < .001).
text.formatted: Trial 1 strongly predicted Trial 2 performance (β = .62, 95% CI [.47, .77], p < .001).

text.text: The HC3 omnibus condition test was significant [F(2, 117) = 3.69, p = .028, with ΔR² = .039] in the corresponding ordinary variance decomposition.
Supporting H1, adjusted Trial 2 performance was 1.84 points higher for the supportive condition than for the neutral control (95% CI [0.47, 3.20], Holm-adjusted p = .026).
The outcome-standardized contrast was 0.46 (95% CI [0.12, 0.79]).
Contrary to H2, the thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise (b = 0.43, 95% CI [-0.83, 1.70], standardized contrast = 0.11, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.42], Holm-adjusted p = .498; Table 2).
text.formatted: Contrary to H2, the thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise (b = 0.43, 95% CI [-0.83, 1.70], standardized contrast = 0.11, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.42], Holm-adjusted p = .498; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Neither a joint test of Condition × Trial 1 slopes (p = .910) nor a quadratic Trial 1 term (p = .983) indicated a violation of the linear common-slope specification.
Self-reported need satisfaction moved in the intended directions.

Relative to the neutral control, participants assigned to the supportive condition reported more overall need satisfaction (b = 0.61, 95% CI [0.32, 0.90]), whereas those assigned to the thwarting condition reported less (b = -0.73, 95% CI [-1.03, -0.43]), both Holm-adjusted ps < .001.

text.text: However, these reports were collected after Trial 2.
They therefore cannot be treated as measures of need frustration or as mediators of performance.
The supportive-control estimate remained positive and similar across baseline-adjusted covariate, scoring, resampling, and influence checks.
Adjustment for sex and experimenter did not attenuate the estimate (b = 2.05, 95% CI [0.68, 3.42], Holm-adjusted p = .011).

The point estimate was also positive when raw change was analyzed, but multiplicity-adjusted evidence was weaker: The change-score contrast had Holm-adjusted p = .097, and the Trial × Condition interaction had p = .068.
Full robustness results and exploratory resilience analyses appear in the supplement.
The present study tested whether brief need-supportive and need-thwarting interactions affect subsequent task performance.
The results supported H1 but not H2.

After initial performance was taken into account, a brief, multicomponent interpersonal condition intended to support autonomy, competence, and relatedness was followed by higher performance compared to performance of those experiencing a neutral interaction.
The thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise.
This finding extends earlier experiments using the same word-generation paradigm in a specific way.
Prior work introduced need-relevant instructions before task performance or combined performance across trials (Sheldon & Filak, 2008; Szulawski et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Prior work introduced need-relevant instructions before task performance or combined performance across trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Sheldon & Filak, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Szulawski et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Here, explicit condition-specific content was introduced only between trials, and subsequent performance was evaluated conditional on performance before the manipulation.
This temporal separation suggests that a brief socio-motivational context may carry over to what people are able to do next.
Post-task need-satisfaction reports were also consistent with the intended manipulation.
Together, these findings are consistent with the SDT proposition that needsupportive social environments can promote effective functioning.
Several design features narrow this interpretation.
Experimenters were aware of the condition because they delivered its interpersonal content.

Training, scripted delivery, monitoring during data collection, administration of all conditions by every experimenter, and an experimenter-adjusted sensitivity analysis address some delivery heterogeneity.
However, without fidelity ratings these features cannot eliminate expectancy or unmeasured delivery effects.
Other limitations concern timing and scope.
Need reports were collected after performance, the design lacked a no-stress control condition, and the stress induction was designed for this study and was not pre-validated.
Furthermore, the word-generation task is not a validated measure of broad performance adaptation, and the sample predominantly consisted of female undergraduates, limiting generalizability.
Moreover, the study had limited sensitivity to small differences, so the null thwarting-control contrast should not be read as evidence of equivalence.
Future work should thus include a stronger need-thwarting manipulation, assess protocol fidelity, and measure motivational states immediately after the manipulation.
That being said, self-reports suggest the need-thwarting manipulation had the intended need-related effect.
It could potentially have resulted in unexpected confounds, for example belittlement promoting short-term higher effort.
Hence, perhaps a stronger and more differentiated manipulation is warranted.
